intro: Soybeans leave an Illinois farm on a barge and end up as animal feed across the ocean. A phone made overseas ends up in a store in Naperville. A family from Aurora trades dollars for pesos at an airport counter, and a part-time worker in Peoria wonders why her paycheck is smaller than her hours times her wage. Each of these is a small piece of the world economy, and each one follows rules you can learn.

This last unit of the course takes the tools you already have, opportunity cost, supply and demand, incentives and the measures of the whole economy, and points them at the world. You will see why two countries gain from trading even when one is better at making everything, what a trade deficit does and does not mean, who really pays for a tariff, and why the value of the dollar keeps moving. You will also sort the taxes Americans pay by who carries them, and ask why some countries are so much richer than others.

By the end you will be able to work a two-country trade example with numbers, trace a tariff or a change in the exchange rate to the people it helps and hurts, compute an average tax rate and say whether a tax is progressive, regressive or proportional, and explain the main ingredients of economic growth. Those are the skills behind nearly every argument about trade, taxes and poverty in the news.
bigQuestion: When goods, money and taxes cross borders and paychecks, who gains, who pays, and how can we tell?

timeline.t: Adam Smith publishes The Wealth of Nations and argues for buying abroad what costs more to make at home
David Ricardo explains comparative advantage, the reason both sides gain from trade
The Sixteenth Amendment is ratified, allowing the modern federal income tax
The Smoot-Hawley Tariff raises U.S. tariffs sharply; other countries retaliate and world trade shrinks
The Bretton Woods conference sets up a system of fixed exchange rates tied to the dollar
Countries sign the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and begin rounds of tariff cuts
The United States stops trading dollars for gold, and major currencies soon begin to float
The North American Free Trade Agreement removes most tariffs among the U.S., Canada and Mexico
The World Trade Organization replaces the GATT as a permanent body in Geneva
China joins the World Trade Organization, reshaping world manufacturing
The United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement replaces NAFTA

words.d: being able to make more of a good than another producer with the same amount of resources
being able to make a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer
the extra goods and services both sides get when they specialize and trade instead of making everything themselves
a negative trade balance; a country's imports are larger than its exports
a tax a government charges on goods imported from other countries
a legal limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported during a period
the price of one country's currency measured in another country's currency
to rise in value; a currency appreciates when it buys more of another currency than before
a tax that takes a larger share of income from higher-income people than from lower-income people
a tax that takes a smaller share of income from higher-income people than from lower-income people
the skills, education, experience and health that make workers productive
the laws, courts, customs and government rules that shape how people can own, trade and invest

test.q: In one hour Country A makes 6 bags or 3 hats. Country B makes 2 bags or 2 hats. Who has the comparative advantage in hats?
choices: Country B, because a hat costs it only 1 bag
Country A, because it makes more hats per hour
Country A, because a hat costs it 2 bags
test.why: A hat costs A 6 divided by 3, or 2 bags; it costs B 2 divided by 2, or 1 bag. B's opportunity cost is lower.

test.q: In the same example, which country has the absolute advantage in both goods?
test.why: Country A makes more bags (6 versus 2) and more hats (3 versus 2) per hour, so it has the absolute advantage in both.

test.q: Two countries trade at a price that lies between their two opportunity costs. What happens?
choices: Only the country with the absolute advantage gains
Both countries can end up with more than they could make alone
Neither gains; trade only moves goods around
test.why: Any price between the two opportunity costs lets each side get a good more cheaply than making it itself.

test.q: A country exports $900 billion and imports $1,100 billion. Its trade balance is
test.why: Exports minus imports is $900 billion minus $1,100 billion, or negative $200 billion, a deficit.

test.q: A U.S. trade deficit is matched by
choices: foreigners investing in or lending to the United States
a fall in U.S. GDP of the same amount
test.why: Dollars spent on imports come back as purchases of American assets such as bonds, stocks and buildings.

test.q: An imported $60 toaster faces a 25% tariff. If the whole tariff passes through, the store price becomes
test.why: 25% of $60 is $15, so the price rises to $75.

test.q: Compared with a tariff that raises the price by the same amount, a quota sends the extra money to
choices: the holders of the import rights
test.why: Under a quota, whoever may import buys at the world price and sells at the higher domestic price, keeping the gap.

test.q: A tariff protects 500 jobs and costs consumers $100 million a year. The cost per job saved is
test.why: $100,000,000 divided by 500 jobs is $200,000 per job.

test.q: Which argument for protection says the barrier should be temporary?
test.why: The infant industry argument protects a new industry only until it grows strong enough to compete.

test.q: The exchange rate moves from 20 to 16 pesos per dollar. A 400-peso hotel room now costs an American
choices: $20, because peso prices did not change
test.why: 400 divided by 16 is $25, up from 400 divided by 20, or $20. Fewer pesos per dollar means a weaker dollar.

test.q: The dollar weakens sharply. Which Illinois business is most likely to gain?
choices: A family planning a trip abroad
A factory that buys foreign motors
A machinery maker that sells abroad
test.why: A weaker dollar makes American goods cheaper in foreign currency, so exporters sell more.

test.q: Eli earns $20,000 and pays $2,000 in a tax. Fay earns $60,000 and pays $6,000. This tax is
test.why: Each pays 10% of income. The same share at every income is proportional.

test.q: Income up to $10,000 is taxed at 10% and income above that at 20%. A person earning $30,000 has an average tax rate of about
test.why: Tax is $1,000 plus 20% of $20,000, which is $4,000, for $5,000 total. $5,000 divided by $30,000 is about 17%.

test.q: Which of these is physical capital rather than human capital?
choices: A container crane at a port
test.why: Physical capital is machines, buildings and equipment; the others are skills held by workers.

test.q: Why do economists say poverty and inequality are different problems?
choices: Because inequality can only fall when poverty rises
Because poverty is only measured in poor countries
Because poverty can fall while the gap between rich and poor grows
test.why: Poverty is about having too little; inequality is about how far apart incomes are. Fast growth can cut one and raise the other.

write.prompt: Illinois soybean farmers face a new foreign tariff, while Congress weighs a 25% U.S. tariff on imported steel that protects mill jobs. Use comparative advantage, tariff arithmetic, cost per job saved and possible retaliation to argue whether the steel tariff is a good idea, naming who gains and who pays.
tips: Put numbers on it: show the price with and without the tariff, and compute a cost per job saved from example figures.
Name who gains (mills, the treasury) and who pays (steel users, consumers), including industries that use steel as an input.
Trace retaliation: which Illinois exports might another country target, and what happens to their sales?
Give the strongest argument on the other side, such as national security or time for workers to adjust, before stating your conclusion.
End with the trade-off you accept and why, in one or two sentences.
